content: Salmonella bongori is a pathogenic bacterium that belongs to the genus Salmonella. It was previously referred to as Salmonella subspecies V, Salmonella enterica subsp. bongori, or Salmonella choleraesuis subsp. bongori. This bacterium is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped organism (bacillus) that causes a gastrointestinal disease known as salmonellosis. The disease is characterized by symptoms such as abdominal cramping and diarrhea. Unlike other members of the Salmonella genus, Salmonella bongori is primarily associated with cold-blooded animals, particularly reptiles. It was first identified in 1966 from a lizard in the city of Bongor, Chad, which is the origin of its specific name, bongori. After years of debate regarding its classification, it was officially recognized as a distinct species in 2005. Salmonella bongori is traditionally considered the Salmonella species associated with lizards. However, studies have shown that it is not strictly host-specific, as it has also been detected in dogs and birds. In animals, infections caused by Salmonella bongori are generally asymptomatic and do not produce noticeable effects, unlike infections caused by other Salmonella species. However, in pet animals, infections have been linked to diarrhea. Human infections with Salmonella bongori have also been documented, with confirmed cases reported in Italy. Most human cases occur in children under the age of three, who are more likely to come into contact with animal feces through oral exposure. Infected individuals typically present with symptoms such as diarrhea, fever, and acute enteritis. The earliest documented human cases were observed in Messina and Palermo in late 1984, followed by reports from other cities in Sicily. Initially, Salmonella bongori was classified as a subspecies within the genus Salmonella. However, based on DNA analysis, all members of the genus are now grouped into only two species: Salmonella bongori and Salmonella enterica. Salmonella species are closely related to Escherichia coli (E. coli), and it is estimated that they diverged from a common ancestor approximately 100 million years ago. Despite this divergence, their genomes still exhibit significant similarities, including many shared functional genes. Genes unique to Salmonella serovars, as compared to E. coli, are often located on large genomic regions known as Salmonella pathogenicity islands (SPIs). These regions encode functions critical for virulence and are key to distinguishing Salmonella enterica from Salmonella bongori. For example, the SPI-2 gene, which encodes a type III secretion system essential for the virulence of Salmonella enterica, is absent in Salmonella bongori. Additionally, some virulence determinants, particularly effector proteins, appear to be more closely related to those found in enteropathogenic E. coli, as certain genes present in Salmonella enterica are missing in Salmonella bongori.
